content.title: Mapping the Global Energy Divide
content.intro: M2: Energy Access and Inclusive Energy Services

content.text:
The global energy landscape is marked by a profound disparity in access to energy services, chiefly manifested between regions and countries. This disparity is often referred to as the 'Global Energy Gap' - or 'Global Energy Divide'.

While some countries have achieved near-universal access to electricity and clean cooking 💬️, others continue to struggle with significant deficits.

This lesson introduces the concept of the global energy divide, tracing progress and disparities across regions, income groups, and geographies.

By mapping the current landscape, it highlights the urgent need for tailored, inclusive, and resilient solutions to ensure no one is left behind in the energy transition.

content.title: Key Concepts
content.intro: Explore foundational ideas from this lesson.

concepts.title: energy access for informal settlements
concepts.body: Energy access for informal settlements refers to the availability and affordability of reliable energy services, such as electricity and clean cooking fuels, for residents living in unplanned or informal housing areas, ensuring they can meet their basic energy needs and improve their quality of life.

concepts.title: energy in crisis settings
concepts.body: Energy in crisis settings refers to the provision and management of energy resources in areas affected by emergencies, such as natural disasters, armed conflicts, or humanitarian crises, where access to reliable energy is critical for survival, recovery, and rebuilding efforts.

concepts.title: global energy gap
concepts.body: The global energy gap refers to the disparity between the world's energy demand and the available energy supply, highlighting the need for increased energy production and sustainable solutions to meet future energy needs.

content.text:
The Global Energy Access Gap refers to the stark disparity between regions, countries, or communities in accessing reliable, affordable, and modern energy services.

This divide reinforces economic inequality, restricts development opportunities, and worsens poverty. The gap is composed of cumulative layers that further entrench inequalities, making energy access a deeply structural challenge. With the added pressures of climate change, these disparities will only intensify if not swiftly addressed. Each layer presents unique characteristics, requiring tailored solutions to meet the distinct needs and contexts of different regions and communities.

content.intro: M2: Energy Access and Inclusive Energy Services
content.title: A: Regions with Quasi-Universal Access

content.text:
In some regions of the world, energy access challenges are a thing of the past. These countries have achieved near-universal access to both electricity and clean cooking. This section highlights the status and key characteristics of high-access regions, showing what is possible with sustained investment and policy support.


High-income regions such as Northern America, Europe, Australia, New Zealand, and much of East Asia have achieved near-universal access to both electricity and clean cooking.

As of 2023, the global electricity access rate reached 92%, and in high-income countries, access typically exceeds 99% for both electricity and clean fuels (IEA., 2024).

In Europe and Central Asia, for example, the electricity access rate was virtually 100%, while the clean cooking access rate stood at 98%.

Similarly, countries like Japan and South Korea have universal energy access, thanks to strong infrastructure, supportive regulatory frameworks, and robust financial systems.
The typical energy access in high income countries

In China, electricity access is nearly universal, and the country has made remarkable progress in clean cooking, with some key caveats that will be explored later in this chapter. Between 2010 and 2022, China contributed to 28% of the global increase in clean cooking access. The country’s access rate to clean fuels and technologies reached over 88.7% by 2023, thanks to large-scale government programs promoting LPG and electricity-based cooking.

In Latin America and the Caribbean, the electricity access rate reached 98.5% in 2023, while clean cooking access stood at 88.8%, with countries like Brazil, Chile, and Costa Rica nearing 100% in both metrics.

Urban areas in these regions show the highest access rates. In urban Latin America, for example, electricity access exceeds 99%, while clean cooking access stands at 94.2%. The widespread use of LPG and electricity in cooking, coupled with high income levels and urban density, has facilitated these gains.


The experience of these regions highlights the importance of strong institutional capacity, integrated planning, and stable financial support.


Furthermore, universal access in these regions is supported by targeted subsidies for vulnerable populations, which ensures that energy remains affordable for all. In high-income countries, energy access has progressed hand in hand with relative policy stability, infrastructure resilience, and widespread consumer trust in public services.

Despite high electrification rates in high income countries, pockets of the population continue to face barriers to affordable and reliable electricity and clean cooking services.

content.intro: M2: Energy Access and Inclusive Energy Services
content.title: B: Regions on a Fast Track to Energy Access

content.text:
Several low- and middle-income countries have made significant progress in expanding electricity and clean cooking access over the past decade. India, for instance, accounted for 42% of the global progress in clean cooking access between 2010 and 2023. India’s clean cooking access rate increased from 30% in 2010 to 74% in 2023. The country also achieved nearly universal electricity access, with less than 1% of its population without power in 2023.

Bangladesh also made significant strides, increasing electricity access from less than 35% in 2000 to nearly 99.5% by 2023. Its clean cooking access rate, however, remains low at 28.4%, highlighting a need for further investment in cooking transitions. Indonesia, represent another story of progress with an increase in clean cooking access rate from 40% in 2010 to 90.6% in 2023.

Pakistan improved from 41.8% to 54.9% in clean cooking access in the last decade, representing 3% of global progress.

In contrast to regions where universal access has been achieved, some countries have made exceptional progress in recent years. This section focuses on those "rapid progress" regions where access to electricity and clean cooking is expanding rapidly due to strong policies, investment, and innovation.

In Africa, Rwanda and Kenya have achieved significant gains in electrification. Rwanda increased electricity access from 15% in 2010 to 63.9% in 2023, while Kenya moved from 28% to 76% over the same period. However, both countries continue to struggle with clean cooking, with access rates of 31% for Kenya and 9% for Rwanda in 2023.

Overall, the average annual increase in electrification globally was 0.77 percentage points between 2010 and 2020, but slowed to 0.39 percentage points between 2020 and 2023.

In contrast, countries like India and Bangladesh had strong momentum, with 40.1 million new connections annually in South Asia during 2020–2022.

These examples show that political will, coordinated investment, and decentralized energy solutions can catalyze rapid improvements.

content.intro: M2: Energy Access and Inclusive Energy Services
content.title: C: Regions with the Greatest Energy Access Deficits

content.text: While some regions are rapidly progressing toward universal energy access, others are falling behind. This section highlights areas where the majority of people still lack basic energy services, particularly in Sub-Saharan Africa and fragile states. Some of these regions face persistent barriers such as political instability, lack of access to financing, and weak institutions.

Sub-Saharan Africa remains the region most significantly lagging behind on energy access. In 2023, only 42.7% of the population had access to electricity, and just 21% had access to clean cooking fuels and technologies. This means around 565 million people in the region still lacked electricity, and over 955 million were dependent on traditional biomass 💬️, charcoal, or kerosene for cooking. The region now accounts for 85% of the global electricity access deficit, up from 50% in 2010.

Annual population growth in Sub-Saharan Africa, around 29.2 million people per year, is nearly equal to the annual increase in electricity access, which was 30.2 million between 2021 and 2023. This parity slows overall progress and highlights the need for faster electrification.

Among the 20 countries with the largest energy access deficits, 18 are in Sub-Saharan Africa, with Nigeria (86.9 million), Democratic Republic of Congo (79.6 million), and Ethiopia (56.4 million) with the highest number of people lacking access, due notably to their large population.

Clean cooking access in Sub-Saharan Africa continues to face significant challenges.

Of the 20 countries with the largest clean cooking access deficits, 8 had access rates below 10% in 2022. These include Ethiopia, Madagascar, Mozambique, Niger, and Uganda. Projections show that over 1 billion people in the region could still be without clean cooking by 2030 if current trends persist.

Progress is also limited in fragile and conflict-affected settings️. In these contexts, access to electricity was 57% in 2023, up from 46% in 2010. However, the absolute number of people without access increased slightly from 427 million in 2020 to 429 million in 2022 due to rapid population growth, limited infrastructure development as well as the social and economic consequences of the COVID 19 pandemic. content.text:
While Sub-Saharan Africa accounts for the vast majority of the global electricity access deficit, challenges persist in other regions as well—particularly in parts of Asia and Oceania.

In Myanmar, about 24% of the population lacked access to electricity in 2023, with rural electrification lagging significantly behind urban areas due to conflict and political upheaval (World Bank, 2023). In Papua New Guinea, the access rate remains among the lowest outside Africa, with just 20% of the population connected to electricity (IEA, 2025). Similarly, in Haiti, only 51% of people had access to electricity in 2023, with significant reliability issues and frequent blackouts compounding the problem (World Bank, 2025).
In Central Asia, although electrification rates are generally high, remote populations often suffer from low-quality or intermittent service that is not captured in headline access statistics.



While global electricity access has improved over the past two decades, stark disparities persist, particularly in Sub-Saharan Africa. Rapid population growth, inadequate institutions, financial constraints, and geographic barriers all continue to slow progress in these regions.

This lesson has shown that the global energy divide is not a single gap, but a layered and evolving challenge that spans regions, income levels, and vulnerability contexts. Achieving universal energy access will require nuanced, region-specific strategies that go beyond connections to address affordability, reliability, and long-term resilience.

takeaways.title: The energy divide is not one gap, but mutiple.
takeaways.description: Energy access varies dramatically across and within countries. While high-income regions have achieved near-universal access, many middle-income and emerging economies are progressing rapidly—yet still face challenges, particularly in clean cooking. At the same time, large parts of the world remain underserved, reinforcing patterns of poverty and exclusion.

takeaways.title: Progress is possible—but uneven.
takeaways.description: Examples from countries like India, Bangladesh, and Rwanda show that rapid gains in electricity access are achievable with strong policy leadership, investment, and innovation. However, clean cooking transitions are lagging even in fast-progressing countries, and rural areas continue to fall behind urban ones in both electricity and cooking services.

takeaways.title: Effective energy access solutions must be tailored to specific local needs and cultural contexts
takeaways.description: Addressing these varied contexts requires flexible, inclusive approaches that incorporate community engagement, recognize cultural values, and offer innovative, sustainable solutions suited to each environment.
